Forecast Projection and Decision Regret:
Theory and Evidence from Battery Arbitrage

Debangana Mukherjee  ††thanks: School of Interwoven Arts and Sciences, Krea University, Sri City, India (debangana.mukherjee@krea.edu.in).    Akash Ashirbad Panda  ††thanks: Corresponding author. Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology Indore, Simrol, India (akashpanda@iiti.ac.in).
Abstract

Decision-focused learning trains forecasts for the decisions they lead to, but forecasts are often projected onto known bounds before use. We study the resulting mismatch in battery arbitrage. When a battery starts and ends the day at the same charge level, a common shift in prices affects its schedule only through round-trip losses. As a result, decision-focused losses identify the forecast level only weakly. For the SPO+ and perturbed Fenchel–Young losses, we characterize the preferred level by a throughput-matching condition. Projecting forecasts onto a price cap can then remove profitable spreads and increase regret, even as prediction error falls. We give bounds on the change in regret, a dual-threshold condition under which a raw-optimal schedule remains optimal after clipping, and a general version of the mechanism for other problems with a conservation constraint. On 1,158 holdout days of the Indian day-ahead market, an equal-weight average of three statistical forecasts outperforms the five decision-focused variants tested. On 53 later days, with 62% of price blocks at the cap, no variant outperforms the regression or the equal-weight average, although most differences from the average are not significant. The results suggest that forecast post-processing should be treated as part of the predict-then-optimize pipeline.

Keywords: decision-focused learning; forecast post-processing; energy storage

MSC2020: 90C31 (primary); 90C05, 90C25, 90B05, 68T05, 62M20, 91B74 (secondary)

1 Introduction

Decision-focused learning (DFL) trains a forecast to improve the decision obtained from an optimization model rather than to minimize prediction error alone (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022; Mandi et al., 2024), including in energy storage (Sang et al., 2022; Smets et al., 2025a; Smets et al., 2025b; Smets et al., 2026). A forecast, however, need not be used in its raw form: it may first be projected onto known price, demand or capacity bounds; more generally, forecasts are often transformed by clipping, truncation, censoring, rounding or normalization before they are used. We ask whether a forecast direction that is nearly irrelevant to the training loss can become important to the decision after this projection.

In electricity markets such bounds are often regulatory. The ordinary day-ahead market of the Indian Energy Exchange had a ceiling of Rs 12/kWh from April 2022, lowered to Rs 10/kWh from 4 April 2023 (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2022a; Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2022b; Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2023a). Cutting forecast prices above the cap down to the cap before scheduling is a natural choice, because actual prices cannot be higher and the change can only reduce the error in each block; the cap does not, however, force the operator to do it.

Consider a price-taking battery with feasible schedules z∈ℱz\in\mathcal{F}, net discharge q⁡(z)q(z), operating cost C⁡(z)C(z), and realized price vector p∈[p¯,p¯]Hp\in[\underline{p},\bar{p}]^{H}. For block length Δ\Delta, its profit and perfect-information value are

J⁡(p,z)=Δ​p⊤​q​(z)−C⁡(z),Π⋆​(p)=maxz∈ℱ⁡J⁡(p,z).J(p,z)=\Delta p^{\top}q(z)-C(z),\qquad\Pi^{\star}(p)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(p,z). (1)

Given a raw forecast uu, the operator uses the box projection g​(u)=Πℬ​(u)g(u)=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(u) onto ℬ=[p¯,p¯]H\mathcal{B}=[\underline{p},\bar{p}]^{H} and selects zg​(u)∈arg​maxz∈ℱ⁡J​(g⁡(u),z)z_{g}(u)\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(g(u),z). The relevant loss in operation is the deployed regret

ℛg​(p,u)=Π⋆​(p)−J⁡(p,zg​(u)),\mathcal{R}^{g}(p,u)=\Pi^{\star}(p)-J\bigl(p,z_{g}(u)\bigr), (2)

which need not follow the prediction error of g⁡(u)g(u), nor the decision-focused loss evaluated at uu.

The key mechanism is a conservation identity. If the battery ends the day at its initial charge, has round-trip efficiency η\eta, and charges T⁡(z)=Δ​∑tctT(z)=\Delta\sum_{t}c_{t} MWh, then

Δ​𝟏⊤​q​(z)=−(1−η)​T​(z),J⁡(p+k​𝟏,z)=J⁡(p,z)−k⁡(1−η)​T​(z).\Delta\mathbf{1}^{\top}q(z)=-(1-\eta)T(z),\qquad J(p+k\mathbf{1},z)=J(p,z)-k(1-\eta)T(z). (3)

Common price shifts therefore leave the raw optimization problem unchanged when η=1\eta=1; when η<1\eta<1, they alter the profit of each feasible schedule only through its charged throughput. For the SPO+ loss, the expected loss along u+k​𝟏u+k\mathbf{1} is convex, and its minimizing shifts satisfy the throughput-matching condition

𝔼​T−​(2​u−p+2​k​𝟏)≤𝔼​T​(z⋆)≤𝔼​T+​(2​u−p+2​k​𝟏),\mathbb{E}\,T^{-}(2u-p+2k\mathbf{1})\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}\,T^{+}(2u-p+2k\mathbf{1}), (4)

where the expectation is over forecasts and prices, T−T^{-} and T+T^{+} are the minimum and maximum charging throughputs of optimal helper schedules, and z⋆z^{\star} is optimal at the realized prices. Under an explicit excess-throughput condition (Assumption 2), this shift is positive; the same mechanism has a perturbed Fenchel–Young counterpart (Theorem 3). Squared-error regularization constrains the population-optimal shift (Corollary 1), whereas incomplete training can create a much larger out-of-sample level error: about Rs 2,450/MWh with 150 training steps per refit in our data, falling to about 430 with 5,000 steps (Section 5).

Projection breaks the near-invariance in (3). Although |g​(u)t−pt|≤|ut−pt||g(u)_{t}-p_{t}|\leq|u_{t}-p_{t}| for every block, clipping can remove the price spreads that determine profitable trades. For example, with realized prices (5,10)(5,10), forecast (7,14)(7,14), cap 1010, no energy loss and a total cost of buying and selling of 44, clipping reduces the mean squared error from 1010 to 22 but changes realized trading profit from 11 to 00. More generally, with no energy loss, a raw forecast can have zero unregularized SPO+ loss while its projected schedule loses the entire available arbitrage profit (Theorem 2).

1.1 Related literature

Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) proposed the SPO+ loss for problems with linear objectives. Berthet et al. (2020) and Blondel et al. (2020) proposed perturbed optimizers and Fenchel–Young losses. Mandi et al. (2024) review the area. Other work asks when it is better to train for accuracy first and optimize later. Hu et al. (2022) show that this simple approach can work very well when the regression is accurate, and Elmachtoub et al. (2023) compare the two approaches. Bertsimas and Kallus (2020) study how to use data directly for decisions. Lee et al. (2026) treat prediction directions that do not affect decisions with a geometric approach that projects the prediction error onto a tangent space. In our problem the forecast level is such a direction when η=1\eta=1, and nearly so when η<1\eta<1; anchoring removes it from training in a similar spirit. Our work adds three things for this setting. First, when η<1\eta<1 the direction is only nearly irrelevant, and the loss has a definite preferred value along it, which we characterize (throughput matching). Second, this preferred value moves away from the accurate level; for the pure loss the shift grows like 1/(1−η)1/(1-\eta) if the matching cost increase stays bounded away from zero, and with a squared-error term it stays bounded. Third, a separate step after the forecast, projection to the price cap, makes this direction matter for decisions.

Sang et al. (2022) train price forecasts for battery trading with a decision-focused loss. Smets et al. (2025a); Smets et al. (2025b); Smets et al. (2026) study value-oriented and proxy-based DFL for batteries. Yi et al. (2025) use perturbed optimizers for battery bidding, and Toubeau et al. (2021) schedule batteries in energy and reserve markets. Alkhulaifi et al. (2026) report strong results for DFL in energy storage with automated feature engineering, in a different setting from ours; our contrasting results suggest that the value of DFL depends on the market and on how the forecast is used. Matsumoto and Sasanuma (2026) show that forecast noise leads to excessive battery trading and that conservative safety margins (guard bands) reduce this optimizer’s curse (Smith and Winkler, 2006). This is a closely related economic explanation of the overtrading in Assumption 2. Our contribution is different: we characterize exactly where the SPO+ and Fenchel–Young losses place the forecast level (throughput matching), show that this works like an implicit safety margin (Remark 2), and study how it interacts with projection to a price cap. As far as we know, none of these studies looks at price caps, at how well the forecast level is learned, or at comparisons with forecast averages.

Weron (2014) and Lago et al. (2021) review price forecasting and propose the LEAR and DNN benchmarks. Maciejowska et al. (2026) argue that forecasts should be judged by their economic value, not only by accuracy. Work on combining forecasts (Bates and Granger, 1969; Timmermann, 2006) shows that equal weights are hard to beat (Smith and Wallis, 2009). We find the same for decisions: weights chosen from past profit do not outperform equal weights.

Sioshansi et al. (2009), Antweiler (2021) and Mercier et al. (2023) measure the value of battery trading and how it depends on forecasts and market rules. We add evidence on how a price cap changes the value of different forecasting methods.

1.2 Contributions

Neither the convexity of SPO+ nor the energy balance of a battery is new. What is new is how they interact with a step that changes the forecast after training and before dispatch.

On the theory side, Theorem 3 gives the price level that minimizes the expected SPO+ loss through the matching condition (4). It shows when this level lies above the accurate level and how it depends on efficiency, and Corollary 1 shows how a squared-error term limits it. Theorem 1 states the same mechanism for any decision problem with Δ​r⊤​q​(z)=−a​T​(z)+b\Delta\,r^{\top}q(z)=-a\,T(z)+b and bounded TT, for example a flexible load that must buy a fixed amount of energy. Lee et al. (2026) study prediction directions that do not affect decisions; we study what happens when the forecast is changed after training.

We also study regret after projection. A raw forecast can have zero SPO+ loss and still have positive regret once it is clipped (Theorem 2), so a regret bound for the raw loss does not carry over to the deployed forecast. Proposition 3 gives the exact condition, in the form of a normal cone, under which any post-processing step keeps a raw-optimal decision optimal, and bounds the change in regret when it does not. Theorem 4 gives a simpler sufficient condition for batteries that can be read off the dual solution of the raw problem, and Corollary 3 deals with ties between equally good schedules. These results add to storage guard-band methods (Matsumoto and Sasanuma, 2026) rather than replace them.

We then propose a simple fix. Taking the forecast level from a separate model, which we call anchoring, stops training from moving the level (Corollary 4). In exploratory comparisons (Section 5.5), anchoring decision-focused forecasts every day worked better than anchoring only when the certificate failed, statistical forecasts did best with their own level, and keeping the raw schedule whenever it remained optimal made the deployed regret equal to the raw regret.

Finally, we test the mechanism on 1,158 holdout days of the Indian day-ahead market and on 53 later days in which most prices were at the cap, and compare with a German market in which the limits do not bind (Section EC.3). An equal-weight average of three statistical forecasts has the lowest regret on the long holdout, 0.47 [0.34, 0.59] lakh per MW-year less than the best DFL variant, or about 0.7% of the perfect-foresight profit. The fresh test gives no sign that any of the tested DFL variants does better. These findings are about the DFL implementations we tested, not about DFL methods in general.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the battery dispatch problem, projection and regret. Section 3 gives the theory. Section 4 describes the data and test design, Section 5 gives the results, and Section 6 discusses what they mean and their limits. The electronic companion contains the proofs (Section EC.1), implementation details (Section EC.2), the German test (Section EC.3), further results (Section EC.4) and the details of the operating rules (Section EC.5).

2 Battery dispatch, projection and regret

A delivery day has HH blocks, each Δ\Delta hours long (for the IEX, H=96H=96 and Δ=0.25\Delta=0.25). Prices p∈ℝHp\in\mathbb{R}^{H} must lie between a floor and a cap set by the regulator, p∈[p¯,p¯]Hp\in[\underline{p},\bar{p}]^{H}. The battery is small, so it does not affect prices. It has energy capacity BB, power limits c¯\bar{c} (charging) and d¯\bar{d} (discharging), and charging and discharging efficiencies ηc\eta_{c} and ηd\eta_{d}. The round-trip efficiency is η=ηc​ηd\eta=\eta_{c}\eta_{d}. A schedule z=(c,d,x)z=(c,d,x) must satisfy

xt=xt−1+Δ⁡(ηc​ct−dt/ηd),0≤ct≤c¯,0≤dt≤d¯,ct​dt=0,0≤xt≤B,x0=xH=x¯.x_{t}=x_{t-1}+\Delta\big(\eta_{c}c_{t}-d_{t}/\eta_{d}\big),\quad 0\leq c_{t}\leq\bar{c},\quad 0\leq d_{t}\leq\bar{d},\quad c_{t}d_{t}=0,\quad 0\leq x_{t}\leq B,\quad x_{0}=x_{H}=\bar{x}.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the set of such schedules. The condition ct​dt=0c_{t}d_{t}=0 says that the battery cannot charge and discharge in the same block. The battery starts and ends the day at the same level x¯\bar{x}. Buying and selling each pay an exchange fee and a battery wear cost γ\gamma per MWh. The total cost per MWh is ωb=ϕb+γ\omega_{b}=\phi_{b}+\gamma for buying and ωs=ϕs+γ\omega_{s}=\phi_{s}+\gamma for selling. At prices π\pi the schedule earns

J⁡(π,z)=Δ​∑t[(πt−ωs)​dt−(πt+ωb)​ct]=Δ​π⊤​q​(z)−C⁡(z),J(\pi,z)=\Delta\textstyle\sum_{t}\big[(\pi_{t}-\omega_{s})d_{t}-(\pi_{t}+\omega_{b})c_{t}\big]=\Delta\pi^{\top}q(z)-C(z),

where q=d−cq=d-c is the net energy sold in each block and C⁡(z)=Δ​∑t(ωs​dt+ωb​ct)C(z)=\Delta\sum_{t}(\omega_{s}d_{t}+\omega_{b}c_{t}) is the cost. Let Π⋆​(π)=maxz∈ℱ⁡J⁡(π,z)\Pi^{\star}(\pi)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(\pi,z) be the best profit at prices π\pi, and let T⁡(z)=Δ​∑tctT(z)=\Delta\sum_{t}c_{t} be the energy charged during the day.

Without the condition ct​dt=0c_{t}d_{t}=0, the problem is a linear program (LP). The LP can be wrong when prices are very negative: by charging and discharging in the same block, the battery buys energy and loses part of it in conversion, without changing its stored energy. Let

θ=−ωb+η​ωs1−η.\theta=-\frac{\omega_{b}+\eta\,\omega_{s}}{1-\eta}. (5)
Lemma 1 (Exact LP).

If πt>θ\pi_{t}>\theta in every block, every optimal solution of the LP has ct​dt=0c_{t}d_{t}=0 in every block, so it is also optimal for the problem with ct​dt=0c_{t}d_{t}=0. If πt<θ\pi_{t}<\theta in some block, charging and discharging in that block can increase LP profit. If η=1\eta=1 and ωb+ωs>0\omega_{b}+\omega_{s}>0, the LP is exact at every price.

We therefore solve the LP and, if a solution charges and discharges in the same block, solve the problem again with binary variables that rule this out. The LP relaxation is therefore exact only under the price condition of Lemma 1; when helper or training prices can fall below θ\theta, the exact re-solve is needed. With our costs, θ\theta is about −6,780-6{,}780 Rs/MWh in India and −77-77 EUR/MWh in Germany. Section EC.2 reports how often the exact re-solve was needed. All results below hold for ℱ\mathcal{F} with the condition ct​dt=0c_{t}d_{t}=0: the proofs use only that profit is affine in prices and linear in the schedule, that ℱ\mathcal{F} does not depend on prices, and that the convex hull of ℱ\mathcal{F} has finitely many extreme points. We write 𝒱=ext⁡(conv⁡ℱ)\mathcal{V}=\operatorname{ext}(\operatorname{conv}\mathcal{F}) for this finite set. Because ℱ\mathcal{F} is compact, 𝒱⊆ℱ\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{F}, and a profit that is linear in the schedule attains its maximum over ℱ\mathcal{F} at a point of 𝒱\mathcal{V}; every optimization over ℱ\mathcal{F} below can therefore be restricted to 𝒱\mathcal{V}. In particular, Π⋆​(π)=maxz∈𝒱⁡J⁡(π,z)\Pi^{\star}(\pi)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{V}}J(\pi,z) is still convex, as a maximum of finitely many affine functions of prices.

On day D−1D-1 the operator makes a forecast p^\hat{p} using the information ℐD\mathcal{I}_{D} available before bidding. Any forecast price outside the allowed range is moved to the nearest limit, in each block:

Πℬ​(p^)=min⁡{max⁡{p^,p¯},p¯}.\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p})=\min\big\{\max\{\hat{p},\underline{p}\},\bar{p}\big\}. (6)

We call this step projection. We distinguish two kinds of regret.

  • •

    Raw regret. If the operator commits to a schedule z^raw∈arg​maxz∈ℱ⁡J​(p^,z)\hat{z}^{\,\mathrm{raw}}\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(\hat{p},z) that is optimal for the forecast itself, its raw regret is

    ℛraw​(p,p^)=Π⋆​(p)−J⁡(p,z^raw)≥0.\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,\hat{p})=\Pi^{\star}(p)-J(p,\hat{z}^{\,\mathrm{raw}})\geq 0. (7)
  • •

    Regret after projection. If the operator first projects the forecast and then commits to a schedule z^∈arg​maxz∈ℱ⁡J​(Πℬ​(p^),z)\hat{z}\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}),z), the regret is

    ℛclip​(p,p^)=ℛraw​(p,Πℬ​(p^))=Π⋆​(p)−J⁡(p,z^).\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p})=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}\big(p,\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p})\big)=\Pi^{\star}(p)-J(p,\hat{z}). (8)

Both are paid at the actual prices and measure the profit lost compared with knowing the prices in advance. Unless stated otherwise, “regret” means regret after projection, ℛclip\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}, which is what we report. When several schedules are equally good, a fixed rule picks one. Unless a specific rule is stated (Corollary 3 and Section 5.5), the results below hold for any such rule.

An operator has two reasons to project a forecast. First, realized prices always lie in ℬ=[p¯,p¯]H\mathcal{B}=[\underline{p},\bar{p}]^{H}, so projection moves every forecast price weakly closer to the realized one, |Πℬ​(p^)t−pt|≤|p^t−pt||\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p})_{t}-p_{t}|\leq|\hat{p}_{t}-p_{t}| for every block tt, and any error measure that increases with the absolute errors, such as the mean squared or mean absolute error, can only fall. Second, a forecast above the cap predicts a price that cannot occur. Projection is therefore a natural default, and it looks harmless. It is still a modeling choice, not a requirement: the cap restricts realized prices, not the prices an operator feeds into its dispatch model. Our results concern decision-focused forecasts that are projected before dispatch, not every use of DFL in a capped market, and Section 5 also reports results without projection.

A two-period example. Projection can reduce forecast error and still make the decision worse. Take a battery with no energy loss that can buy 1 MWh in period 1 and sell it in period 2. The total buying and selling cost is 4 per MWh. Actual prices are p=(5,10)p=(5,10), the cap is 10, and the forecast is p^=(7,14)\hat{p}=(7,14) (all in the same price unit).

  • •

    Before projection, the forecast spread is 14−7=7>414-7=7>4, so the battery trades. It earns 10−5−4=110-5-4=1.

  • •

    After projection, the forecast is (7,10)(7,10) and the spread is 3<43<4, so the battery does not trade. It earns 0.

Projection lowers the mean squared error of the forecast from 10 to 2, but lowers profit from 1 to 0. The forecast is too high on average, like the DFL forecasts in Section 5, and projection removes the information that period 2 is much more expensive than period 1. This is the main mechanism of the paper, without SPO+ or a 96-block schedule. It also shows that a smaller forecast error does not always give a better decision.

Lemma 2 (Energy balance and price level).

For every z∈ℱz\in\mathcal{F}, Δ​𝟏⊤​q​(z)=−(1−η)​T​(z)\Delta\mathbf{1}^{\top}q(z)=-(1-\eta)\,T(z). Therefore, for all π\pi and k∈ℝk\in\mathbb{R},

J⁡(π+k​𝟏,z)=J⁡(π,z)−k⁡(1−η)​T​(z)=J⁡(π,z,ωb+k⁡(1−η),ωs),J(\pi+k\mathbf{1},z)=J(\pi,z)-k(1-\eta)T(z)=J\big(\pi,z;\ \omega_{b}+k(1-\eta),\ \omega_{s}\big),

and for α>0\alpha>0,

arg​maxz⁡J​(α​π+k​𝟏,z,ωb,ωs)=arg​maxz⁡J​(π,z,(ωb+k⁡(1−η))/α,ωs/α).\argmax_{z}J(\alpha\pi+k\mathbf{1},z;\omega_{b},\omega_{s})=\argmax_{z}J\big(\pi,z;(\omega_{b}+k(1-\eta))/\alpha,\ \omega_{s}/\alpha\big). (9)

Lemma 2 says two things. First, adding the same amount kk to all prices has exactly the same effect as raising the cost of buying by k⁡(1−η)k(1-\eta). When η=1\eta=1 it has no effect at all. Second, scaling and shifting a forecast is the same as changing the buying and selling costs in the LP. So safety margins (Matsumoto and Sasanuma, 2026) and level changes are the same kind of correction.

Proposition 1 (Which forecast errors matter).

Let v=Πℬ​(p^)v=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}) and let e=v−pe=v-p be the error of the projected forecast, with daily mean kk and remaining part e∘=e−k​𝟏e^{\circ}=e-k\mathbf{1}. Let z^\hat{z} be optimal at vv. Then

0≤ℛclip​(p,p^)≤Δ​∑t|et|​|qt⋆−q^t|andℛclip​(p,p^)≤|k|​(1−η)​|T⁡(z⋆)−T⁡(z^)|+Δ​∑t|et∘|​|qt⋆−q^t|.0\leq\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p})\leq\Delta\sum_{t}|e_{t}|\,|q^{\star}_{t}-\hat{q}_{t}|\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p})\leq|k|(1-\eta)\,|T(z^{\star})-T(\hat{z})|+\Delta\sum_{t}|e^{\circ}_{t}|\,|q^{\star}_{t}-\hat{q}_{t}|.

Proposition 1 shows that an error in the forecast level costs money only through the round-trip loss 1−η1-\eta and the difference in charged energy between the two schedules. An error in the shape of the daily curve costs money directly. The forecast level therefore matters little for the decision, as long as nothing changes it later. Section 3 shows that it starts to matter when the forecast is trained on a decision loss and then projected.

Proposition 2 (Regret that can and cannot be reduced).

Let ν=𝔼⁡[p∣ℐD]\nu=\mathbb{E}[p\mid\mathcal{I}_{D}]. For any ℐD\mathcal{I}_{D}-measurable forecast with committed schedule z^\hat{z},

𝔼​ℛclip​(p,p^)=𝔼⁡[Π⋆​(p)−Π⋆​(ν)]+𝔼⁡[Π⋆​(ν)−J⁡(ν,z^)],\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p})=\mathbb{E}\big[\Pi^{\star}(p)-\Pi^{\star}(\nu)\big]+\mathbb{E}\big[\Pi^{\star}(\nu)-J(\nu,\hat{z})\big], (10)

and both terms are nonnegative.

The first term is the value of information that no forecast can recover. The second term comes from the forecasting method, and it is the only part that a better method can reduce. All our comparisons of methods are differences in this second term.

3 Decision-focused learning and forecast post-processing

This section studies how decision-focused losses treat the forecast level and how projection changes the resulting decisions. Section 3.1 defines the two losses, and Section 3.2 states the mechanism for a general decision problem. Sections 3.3 to 3.6 then develop the battery case: the lossless battery, the level shift under energy loss, conditions under which projection preserves a decision, and training on projected forecasts.

3.1 Decision-focused losses

Definition 1 (Decision-focused losses).

Fix a perfect-foresight schedule z⋆∈arg​maxz∈ℱ⁡J​(p,z)z^{\star}\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(p,z). The SPO+ loss (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022), written for our profit-maximization problem, is

ℓ⁡(p^,p)=Π⋆​(2​p^−p)−2​J​(p^,z⋆)+Π⋆​(p),\ell(\hat{p},p)=\Pi^{\star}(2\hat{p}-p)-2J(\hat{p},z^{\star})+\Pi^{\star}(p),

with subgradient 2​Δ​(q⁡(z~)−q⁡(z⋆))2\Delta\big(q(\tilde{z})-q(z^{\star})\big), where z~\tilde{z} is the best schedule at the comparison price 2​p^−p2\hat{p}-p. The perturbed Fenchel–Young loss (Berthet et al., 2020; Blondel et al., 2020) with noise scale σ>0\sigma>0 is

Lσ​(p^,p)=𝔼Z​Π⋆​(p^+σ​Z)−J⁡(p^,z⋆),L_{\sigma}(\hat{p},p)=\mathbb{E}_{Z}\,\Pi^{\star}(\hat{p}+\sigma Z)-J(\hat{p},z^{\star}), (11)

where ZZ is standard normal. Its gradient is Δ⁡(𝔼Z​q​(z^σ)−q⁡(z⋆))\Delta\big(\mathbb{E}_{Z}q(\hat{z}_{\sigma})-q(z^{\star})\big).

Both losses are convex in p^\hat{p}. SPO+ satisfies ℓ⁡(p,p)=0\ell(p,p)=0 and ℓ⁡(p^,p)≥ℛraw​(p,p^)\ell(\hat{p},p)\geq\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,\hat{p}): it bounds the regret of the schedule optimized at the same forecast that enters the loss (Section EC.1). Applied to the projected forecast, this gives ℓ⁡(Πℬ​(p^),p)≥ℛclip​(p,p^)\ell(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}),p)\geq\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p}). In general, ℓ⁡(p^,p)\ell(\hat{p},p) does not bound the regret after projection, ℛclip​(p,p^)\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p}) (Remark 1). In both cases, the gradient compares the schedule of a helper dispatch problem with the perfect-foresight schedule. This comparison drives the results below.

Remark 1 (The raw SPO+ loss can be zero while regret after projection is positive).

Take the two-period example of Section 2: p=(5,10)p=(5,10), p^=(7,14)\hat{p}=(7,14), cap 10, total trading cost 4, no energy loss. The perfect-foresight schedule buys in period 1 and sells in period 2, so Π⋆​(p)=1\Pi^{\star}(p)=1. At the comparison price 2​p^−p=(9,18)2\hat{p}-p=(9,18) the best profit is 18−9−4=518-9-4=5, and J⁡(p^,z⋆)=14−7−4=3J(\hat{p},z^{\star})=14-7-4=3. So

ℓ⁡(p^,p)=5−2⋅3+1=0,ℛraw​(p,p^)=0,ℛclip​(p,p^)=1.\ell(\hat{p},p)=5-2\cdot 3+1=0,\qquad\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,\hat{p})=0,\qquad\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p})=1.

The raw loss is zero, but the deployed (projected) forecast loses all the profit. The bound for the projected forecast does hold: at Πℬ​(p^)=(7,10)\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p})=(7,10) the comparison price is (9,10)(9,10), with best profit 0, and J⁡((7,10),z⋆)=−1J((7,10),z^{\star})=-1, so ℓ⁡(Πℬ​(p^),p)=0+2+1=3≥1\ell(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}),p)=0+2+1=3\geq 1. Theorem 2(ii) below gives the same failure for a whole day of blocks.

3.2 The general mechanism

We first state the mechanism in general: a forecast feeds a decision problem and is post-processed before use. The rest of this section develops the battery case, which is its main instance and for which the structure of storage gives sharper results. Let 𝒵\mathcal{Z} be a compact feasible set whose convex hull has finitely many extreme points, 𝒱𝒵=ext⁡(conv⁡𝒵)\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{Z}}=\operatorname{ext}(\operatorname{conv}\mathcal{Z}) (for example, a polytope, a finite union of polytopes or a bounded mixed-integer set), and let a forecast u∈ℝHu\in\mathbb{R}^{H} give the profit J⁡(u,z)=Δ​u⊤​q​(z)−C⁡(z)J(u,z)=\Delta\,u^{\top}q(z)-C(z), with qq and CC linear in zz. Write Π⋆​(u)=maxz∈𝒵⁡J⁡(u,z)\Pi^{\star}(u)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}J(u,z), and define the SPO+ and perturbed Fenchel–Young losses as in Definition 1. The forecast is deployed after a post-processing map g:ℝH→ℝHg:\mathbb{R}^{H}\to\mathbb{R}^{H}, such as clipping or projection onto bounds, truncation, censoring, rounding or normalization, and its regret is ℛg​(p,u)=Π⋆​(p)−J⁡(p,z^)\mathcal{R}^{g}(p,u)=\Pi^{\star}(p)-J(p,\hat{z}) with z^\hat{z} optimal at g⁡(u)g(u).

Assumption 1 (Near conservation).

There are a direction r∈ℝHr\in\mathbb{R}^{H}, r≠0r\neq 0, a constant a≥0a\geq 0, a constant bb and a linear function TT with values in [0,T¯][0,\bar{T}] on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, where T¯=max𝒵⁡T\bar{T}=\max_{\mathcal{Z}}T, such that

Δ​r⊤​q​(z)=−a​T​(z)+bfor every ​z∈𝒵.\Delta\,r^{\top}q(z)=-a\,T(z)+b\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal{Z}. (12)
Theorem 1 (Weakly identified directions and post-processing).

Under Assumption 1:

  1. (i)

    |ℓ⁡(u+k​v,p)−ℓ⁡(u,p)|≤2​|k|​a​T¯|\ell(u+kv,p)-\ell(u,p)|\leq 2|k|a\bar{T} for all u,p,ku,p,k. If a=0a=0, the SPO+ loss and the raw decision do not depend on the component of the forecast along rr.

  2. (ii)

    If a>0a>0, the expected SPO+ loss along rr is convex, and its minimizers are exactly the shifts kk that satisfy the throughput-matching condition

    𝔼​T−​(2​u^−p+2​k​v)≤𝔼​T​(z⋆)≤𝔼​T+​(2​u^−p+2​k​v),\mathbb{E}\,T^{-}(2\hat{u}-p+2kv)\leq\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})\leq\mathbb{E}\,T^{+}(2\hat{u}-p+2kv), (13)

    where T−T^{-} and T+T^{+} are the smallest and largest values of TT among best decisions at the given forecast. If min𝒵⁡T<𝔼​T​(z⋆)<T¯\min_{\mathcal{Z}}T<\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})<\bar{T}, the minimizers form a nonempty closed and bounded interval. When the helper problem has larger expected TT than the perfect-foresight decision at k=0k=0, every minimizer is positive and equals δ⋆/(2​a)\delta^{\star}/(2a) for a matching cost increase δ⋆\delta^{\star} on TT. If a=0a=0, the expected loss is constant along rr.

  3. (iii)

    With a squared-error term λ​𝔼​[H−1​‖u^+k​v−p‖2]\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[H^{-1}\|\hat{u}+kv-p\|^{2}], λ>0\lambda>0, on the unprocessed forecast, the minimizer kλk_{\lambda} is unique and lies within a​T¯​H/(λ​‖r‖2)a\bar{T}H/(\lambda\|r\|^{2}) of the squared-error minimizer −r⊤𝔼(u^−p)/∥r∥2-r^{\top}\mathbb{E}(\hat{u}-p)/\|r\|^{2}.

  4. (iv)

    Suppose gg saturates along rr at pp: g⁡(p+k​v)=sg(p+kv)=s for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}. If a=0a=0, then ℓ⁡(p+k​v,p)=0\ell(p+kv,p)=0 for every kk, while for k≥k0k\geq k_{0} the deployed regret is that of a best decision at the fixed vector ss, whatever kk is; for the battery with s=p¯​𝟏s=\bar{p}\mathbf{1} this is the whole of Π⋆​(p)\Pi^{\star}(p).

  5. (v)

    Suppose gg acts coordinate by coordinate, g​(u)t=gt​(ut)g(u)_{t}=g_{t}(u_{t}), and let SS be a set of coordinates such that each gtg_{t}, t∈St\in S, is constant on an open interval containing utu_{t}. Then u↦ℓ⁡(g⁡(u),p)u\mapsto\ell(g(u),p) does not change when (ut)t∈S(u_{t})_{t\in S} move within these intervals, so every chain-rule subgradient of it has zero entries in SS. Clipping to a box satisfies this, with SS the coordinates strictly outside the bounds. For maps that mix coordinates, such as projection onto a simplex, saturation of one output coordinate does not imply this. A sufficient local condition for a general map gg that is differentiable at uu is that the whole jj-th column of its Jacobian vanishes, D​g​(u)​ej=0Dg(u)e_{j}=0; then every chain-rule subgradient of ℓ⁡(g⁡(⋅),p)\ell(g(\cdot),p) at uu has a zero jj-th entry.

  6. (vi)

    For any ww with w⊤​r≠0w^{\top}r\neq 0 and any level estimate L^\hat{L}, the anchored forecast u−(w⊤​u/w⊤​r)​r+L^​ru-(w^{\top}u/w^{\top}r)\,r+\hat{L}\,r does not change when uu moves along rr, so training on it cannot learn a shift along rr.

Theorem 1 rests on three assumptions: profit affine in the forecast; a feasible set that does not depend on the forecast and whose convex hull has finitely many extreme points; and the near-conservation identity of Assumption 1 with bounded TT. Parts (i) and (iii), the convexity and matching statements in (ii), and part (vi) follow from these by the same arguments as the battery results below, with 𝟏\mathbf{1} replaced by rr and (1−η)​T(1-\eta)T by a​TaT; the constant bb cancels (Section EC.1). The existence claim in (ii) needs, in addition, that TT attains its minimum and maximum on 𝒱𝒵\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{Z}}, which holds because 𝒱𝒵\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{Z}} is finite, and a dominated-convergence step that uses the bound 0≤T≤T¯0\leq T\leq\bar{T}. Parts (iv) and (v) concern the post-processing map and need only the stated properties of gg. The mechanism is therefore not specific to price caps or to batteries. The theorem says where the problem comes from: a direction in which the decision loss is flat or nearly flat (aa zero or small) combined with a post-processing map that is not neutral along that direction. Two examples besides batteries:

  • •

    Batteries. By Lemma 2, a battery that ends the day at its initial charge satisfies Assumption 1 with r=𝟏r=\mathbf{1}, a=1−ηa=1-\eta, TT its charged energy and b=0b=0. Sections 3.3 to 3.6 develop this case.

  • •

    Flexible load. A process or a fleet of electric vehicles must buy a fixed amount of energy EE over the day, ∑tΔ​xt=E\sum_{t}\Delta x_{t}=E with 0≤xt≤x¯t0\leq x_{t}\leq\bar{x}_{t}, at forecast prices. With r=𝟏r=\mathbf{1} and q⁡(z)=−xq(z)=-x, Assumption 1 holds with a=0a=0, so decision-focused losses carry no information at all about the price level. A two-period example: one unit must be bought in either period, actual prices are (5,10)(5,10) and the cap is 10. The forecast (12,17)(12,17), which is the actual price vector shifted up by 7, has zero SPO+ loss by part (iv) and leads to the correct purchase in period 1. After clipping it becomes (10,10)(10,10), at which both periods are optimal; a solver that picks period 2 pays 10 instead of 5. If every block is clipped, every feasible schedule is optimal at the clipped forecast, and the deployed schedule is decided by tie-breaking alone.

  • •

    Storage with proportional losses. Inventory or a water reservoir with a fixed terminal level and proportional losses satisfies the assumption with aa equal to the loss rate, as the battery does with a=1−ηa=1-\eta.

We test only the battery case.

3.3 Batteries with no energy loss

Theorem 2 (Level invariance and failure after projection).

Let T¯=maxz∈ℱ⁡T⁡(z)\bar{T}=\max_{z\in\mathcal{F}}T(z).

  1. (i)

    For all p^,p\hat{p},p and kk,

    |ℓ⁡(p^+k​𝟏,p)−ℓ⁡(p^,p)|≤2​|k|​(1−η)​T¯.\big|\ell(\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1},p)-\ell(\hat{p},p)\big|\leq 2|k|(1-\eta)\bar{T}. (14)

    In particular, ℓ\ell does not change with the level when η=1\eta=1.

  2. (ii)

    Suppose ωb,ωs>0\omega_{b},\omega_{s}>0, the cap p¯>0\bar{p}>0 is the same in all blocks of the day, p∈[0,p¯]Hp\in[0,\bar{p}]^{H} and Π⋆​(p)>0\Pi^{\star}(p)>0. For every k≥p¯−mint⁡ptk\geq\bar{p}-\min_{t}p_{t}, the projected forecast Πℬ​(p+k​𝟏)=p¯​𝟏\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(p+k\mathbf{1})=\bar{p}\mathbf{1} has idling as its only best schedule. So ℛclip​(p,p+k​𝟏)=Π⋆​(p)\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,p+k\mathbf{1})=\Pi^{\star}(p), while ℓ⁡(p+k​𝟏,p)≤2​k​(1−η)​T¯\ell(p+k\mathbf{1},p)\leq 2k(1-\eta)\bar{T}, which is zero when η=1\eta=1.

  3. (iii)

    Take a model class that allows level shifts (for example, any model with an intercept), and let η=1\eta=1. Then the training SPO+ loss is the same for all level shifts. So some of the models with the lowest training loss give projected forecasts that lose the whole perfect-foresight profit on every training day.

Part (ii) shows the worst case. Its regret statement holds for every η\eta: if every block of the shifted forecast is at or above the cap, the battery does not trade and loses its whole profit. Only the statement that the unregularized SPO+ loss is zero needs η=1\eta=1; it does not cover the regularized objective used in training. As a result, no bound of the form ℛclip​(p,p^)≤ϕ⁡(ℓ⁡(p^,p))\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,\hat{p})\leq\phi(\ell(\hat{p},p)) with ϕ⁡(0)=0\phi(0)=0 can hold for the raw SPO+ loss once forecasts are projected: with η=1\eta=1, part (ii) gives a forecast with zero raw loss whose regret after projection is the whole perfect-foresight profit. A surrogate guarantee for the raw decision problem does not transfer through the deployment map; only the loss evaluated at the deployed, projected forecast bounds the deployed regret. For real batteries (η<1\eta<1), part (i) only bounds how much the loss can change, and does not by itself predict a failure. The next result explains what happens when η<1\eta<1.

3.4 Batteries with energy loss: an upward level shift

For a price vector π\pi, let T−​(π)T^{-}(\pi) and T+​(π)T^{+}(\pi) be the smallest and largest charged energy among the best schedules at π\pi. They are equal when the best schedule is unique.

Lemma 3 (Charging falls as prices rise).

If η<1\eta<1, k1<k2k_{1}<k_{2} and ziz_{i} is a best schedule at π+ki​𝟏\pi+k_{i}\mathbf{1}, then T⁡(z1)≥T⁡(z2)T(z_{1})\geq T(z_{2}).

In all statements about expected losses (Theorem 3, Corollary 1, Proposition 2 and Theorem 1) we assume that prices and forecasts have finite first moments, 𝔼​‖p‖1<∞\mathbb{E}\|p\|_{1}<\infty and 𝔼​‖p^‖1<∞\mathbb{E}\|\hat{p}\|_{1}<\infty, and, where a squared-error term is used, finite second moments. Because the feasible set has finitely many extreme points, |Π⋆​(π)|≤c0+c1​‖π‖1|\Pi^{\star}(\pi)|\leq c_{0}+c_{1}\|\pi\|_{1} for constants c0,c1c_{0},c_{1}, so all losses are integrable, and charged energy is bounded; these facts justify exchanging expectation with one-sided differentiation and limits in the proofs.

Assumption 2 (The helper problem has excess throughput).

At the forecast’s own level, the helper problem charges more energy on average than the perfect-foresight schedule:

𝔼​T−​(2​p^−p)>𝔼​T​(z⋆).\mathbb{E}\,T^{-}(2\hat{p}-p)>\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star}). (15)

Assumption 2 is a condition, not a general property of SPO+. It holds in both of our markets (Section 5 and Section EC.3), but it can fail, for example for a forecast that is too smooth. Without it, Theorem 3 still gives the matching condition, but the best shift can be zero or negative.

Theorem 3 (Loss-minimizing level shift of the SPO+ loss).

Let η<1\eta<1. Fix a forecast rule p^\hat{p} that uses only the information available before bidding, and let Φ⁡(k)=𝔼​ℓ​(p^+k​𝟏,p)\Phi(k)=\mathbb{E}\,\ell(\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1},p) be the expected SPO+ loss when the forecast level is shifted by kk. Let K⋆=arg​mink⁡Φ​(k)K^{\star}=\argmin_{k}\Phi(k).

  1. (i)

    Φ\Phi is convex, with one-sided derivatives

    Φ±′​(k)=−2​(1−η)​𝔼​[T∓​(2​p^−p+2​k​𝟏)−T⁡(z⋆)].\Phi^{\prime}_{\pm}(k)=-2(1-\eta)\,\mathbb{E}\big[T^{\mp}(2\hat{p}-p+2k\mathbf{1})-T(z^{\star})\big]. (16)
  2. (ii)

    Throughput matching. k∈K⋆k\in K^{\star} if and only if

    𝔼​T−​(2​p^−p+2​k​𝟏)≤𝔼​T​(z⋆)≤𝔼​T+​(2​p^−p+2​k​𝟏).\mathbb{E}\,T^{-}(2\hat{p}-p+2k\mathbf{1})\leq\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})\leq\mathbb{E}\,T^{+}(2\hat{p}-p+2k\mathbf{1}). (17)

    The expected charged energy of the helper problem does not increase as kk increases. If 0<𝔼​T​(z⋆)<T¯0<\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})<\bar{T}, then K⋆K^{\star} is a nonempty, closed and bounded interval.

  3. (iii)

    Direction. Under Assumption 2, every k∈K⋆k\in K^{\star} is positive.

  4. (iv)

    Size. For δ∈ℝ\delta\in\mathbb{R}, let Tδ±T^{\pm}_{\delta} be the charged energy (largest and smallest over the best schedules) when the buying cost is raised by δ\delta. Let

    D⋆={δ:𝔼​Tδ−​(2​p^−p)≤𝔼​T​(z⋆)≤𝔼​Tδ+​(2​p^−p)}D^{\star}=\big\{\delta:\ \mathbb{E}\,T^{-}_{\delta}(2\hat{p}-p)\leq\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})\leq\mathbb{E}\,T^{+}_{\delta}(2\hat{p}-p)\big\}

    be the set of matching cost increases. Then K⋆={δ/(2​(1−η)):δ∈D⋆}K^{\star}=\{\delta/(2(1-\eta)):\delta\in D^{\star}\}. If min⁡D⋆≥δ0>0\min D^{\star}\geq\delta_{0}>0 for all η\eta near one, then min⁡K⋆→∞\min K^{\star}\to\infty as η→1\eta\to 1.

  5. (v)

    Fenchel–Young. For LσL_{\sigma}, (i)–(iv) hold with comparison price p^+σ​Z\hat{p}+\sigma Z (and the expectation also taken over ZZ), and with 2​(1−η)2(1-\eta) replaced by 1−η1-\eta.

Remark 2 (Why the helper problem has excess throughput).

The comparison price 2​p^−p=p^+(p^−p)2\hat{p}-p=\hat{p}+(\hat{p}-p) contains the forecast error twice. Errors can make the price differences within the day look larger, so the helper problem may find more profitable cycles than actually exist. The perturbed loss adds noise to the forecast and can have the same effect. Whether this happens depends on the forecast; Assumption 2 states it as a condition. By Lemma 2, raising the level is the same as raising the cost of charging. So DFL uses the forecast level to reduce trading, which works like a safety margin (Matsumoto and Sasanuma, 2026). Without a binding cap this acts as a small trading cost. With a binding cap it pushes the forecast peaks above the cap.

Practical DFL methods, including all five we test, add a squared-error term to the decision loss. The next result covers the case where both terms use the forecast before projection, as in V1. The case where both terms use the forecast after projection, as in V2–V5, is different and is discussed in Remark 3.

Corollary 1 (SPO+ with a squared-error term, before projection).

Let λ>0\lambda>0 and let e¯=𝔼⁡[H−1​𝟏⊤​(p^−p)]\bar{e}=\mathbb{E}\big[H^{-1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}(\hat{p}-p)\big] be the mean forecast error. Let

ℒλ​(k)=Φ⁡(k)+λ​𝔼​[1H​‖p^+k​𝟏−p‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(k)=\Phi(k)+\lambda\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\tfrac{1}{H}\big\|\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1}-p\big\|^{2}\Big],

with both terms in the same money units. Then:

  1. (i)

    ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda} is strictly convex and has a unique minimizer kλk_{\lambda}, given by

    (1−η)​(𝔼​T−​(2​p^−p+2​kλ​𝟏)−𝔼​T​(z⋆))≤λ⁡(kλ+e¯)≤(1−η)​(𝔼​T+​(2​p^−p+2​kλ​𝟏)−𝔼​T​(z⋆)).(1-\eta)\big(\mathbb{E}\,T^{-}(2\hat{p}-p+2k_{\lambda}\mathbf{1})-\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})\big)\ \leq\ \lambda\,(k_{\lambda}+\bar{e})\ \leq\ (1-\eta)\big(\mathbb{E}\,T^{+}(2\hat{p}-p+2k_{\lambda}\mathbf{1})-\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star})\big).
  2. (ii)

    |kλ+e¯|≤(1−η)​T¯/λ|k_{\lambda}+\bar{e}|\leq(1-\eta)\bar{T}/\lambda. So the shift away from the squared-error level −e¯-\bar{e} stays bounded, and it goes to zero as η→1\eta\to 1 or λ→∞\lambda\to\infty. Unlike the minimizer of the pure loss, which can diverge under the condition of Theorem 3(iv), it stays bounded as η→1\eta\to 1.

  3. (iii)

    If the helper problem has excess throughput at the squared-error level, that is, 𝔼​T−​(2​p^−p−2​e¯​𝟏)>𝔼​T​(z⋆)\mathbb{E}\,T^{-}(2\hat{p}-p-2\bar{e}\mathbf{1})>\mathbb{E}\,T(z^{\star}), then kλ>−e¯k_{\lambda}>-\bar{e}: the shift is upward. If, in addition, −e¯<min⁡K⋆-\bar{e}<\min K^{\star}, then −e¯<kλ≤min⁡K⋆-\bar{e}<k_{\lambda}\leq\min K^{\star}.

Remark 3 (Squared error after projection: no guarantee).

In V2–V5, the decision loss and the squared-error term both use the projected forecast:

ℒλproj​(k)=𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Πℬ​(p^+k​𝟏),p)+λH​‖Πℬ​(p^+k​𝟏)−p‖2].\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{proj}}_{\lambda}(k)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\ell\big(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1}),p\big)+\tfrac{\lambda}{H}\big\|\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1})-p\big\|^{2}\Big].

This function is generally not convex in kk, and it is completely flat in kk once every block is clipped (Proposition 4). So Corollary 1 does not apply: there need not be a unique or a bounded loss-minimizing level. The derivative of the penalty is

2​λH𝔼∑tχt(k)(Πℬ(p^+k𝟏)t−pt),χt(k)=𝟏{p¯<p^t+k<p¯},\frac{2\lambda}{H}\,\mathbb{E}\sum_{t}\chi_{t}(k)\big(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1})_{t}-p_{t}\big),\qquad\chi_{t}(k)=\mathbf{1}\{\underline{p}<\hat{p}_{t}+k<\bar{p}\}, (18)

so the penalty gives no pull back in clipped blocks.

Theorem 3 and Corollary 1 describe the optimum of the loss. They do not say that a training algorithm reaches it. In a weakly curved direction, a stochastic optimizer with a limited number of steps can stay far from the optimum. Section 5 shows that this is what happens in our experiments: with more training steps, the level error falls sharply.

3.5 When projection preserves the decision

Let uu be a raw forecast, v=Πℬ​(u)v=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(u) its projection, and 𝒞={t:ut≠vt}\mathcal{C}=\{t:u_{t}\neq v_{t}\} the clipped blocks. Let zuz_{u} be a best schedule at uu and zvz_{v} a best schedule at vv. Projection changes prices only in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and it lowers them in blocks cut at the cap and raises them in blocks raised to the floor.

Proposition 3 (Projection and the decision).
  1. (i)

    Exact condition. zuz_{u} is a best schedule at vv if and only if, for every z∈𝒱z\in\mathcal{V},

    J⁡(u,zu)−J⁡(u,z)≥Δ​∑t∈𝒞(ut−vt)​(qt​(zu)−qt​(z));J(u,z_{u})-J(u,z)\ \geq\ \Delta\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}}(u_{t}-v_{t})\big(q_{t}(z_{u})-q_{t}(z)\big);

    equivalently, vv lies in the normal cone

    N⁡(zu)={π:zu∈arg​maxz∈ℱ⁡J​(π,z)},N(z_{u})=\big\{\pi:z_{u}\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{F}}J(\pi,z)\big\}, (19)

    which is a polyhedron.

  2. (ii)

    Margin condition. Suppose zuz_{u} is the unique best point of 𝒱\mathcal{V} at uu, and for every other z∈𝒱z\in\mathcal{V},

    J⁡(u,zu)−J⁡(u,z)>Δ​∑t∈𝒞|ut−vt|​|qt​(zu)−qt​(z)|.J(u,z_{u})-J(u,z)>\Delta\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}}|u_{t}-v_{t}|\,|q_{t}(z_{u})-q_{t}(z)|.

    Then zuz_{u} is also the unique best schedule at vv, so ℛclip​(p,u)=ℛraw​(p,u)\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,u)=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,u).

  3. (iii)

    Change in regret from projection. For any choice of zuz_{u} and zvz_{v},

    Δ​(p−u)⊤​(q⁡(zu)−q⁡(zv))≤ℛclip​(p,u)−ℛraw​(p,u)≤Δ​(p−v)⊤​(q⁡(zu)−q⁡(zv)).\Delta(p-u)^{\top}\big(q(z_{u})-q(z_{v})\big)\ \leq\ \mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,u)-\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,u)\ \leq\ \Delta(p-v)^{\top}\big(q(z_{u})-q(z_{v})\big).

    The two bounds differ by Δ​∑t∈𝒞(ut−vt)​(qt​(zu)−qt​(zv))≥0\Delta\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}}(u_{t}-v_{t})\big(q_{t}(z_{u})-q_{t}(z_{v})\big)\geq 0, which involves only the clipped blocks.

Part (i) is exact: projection preserves the optimality of zuz_{u} exactly when the change it makes to the forecast keeps the forecast inside the normal cone of zuz_{u}. Parts (i) and (ii) are standard sensitivity arguments. None of the three parts is specific to batteries. They hold for any decision problem whose profit is affine in the forecast and whose feasible set has a convex hull with finitely many extreme points, including mixed-integer sets such as our physical ℱ\mathcal{F}. They also hold for any post-processing map, with 𝒞\mathcal{C} the set of coordinates it changes. Checking (i) or (ii) directly, however, requires a comparison with every point of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, or a new solve at vv. Part (iii) bounds the change in regret caused by projection, which can be positive, negative or zero, because projection can improve as well as worsen a deployed decision. Both bounds depend on forecast errors in all blocks; only the gap between them is confined to the clipped blocks. The next result uses the structure of the battery problem to give a sufficient condition that can be checked block by block from the raw solution alone.

Suppose every price in uu and vv exceeds θ\theta, so the LP is exact (Lemma 1). Let μ\mu be an optimal dual solution of the LP at uu, with μt\mu_{t}, the value of stored energy in block tt, the dual variable of the storage equation of block tt. When the dual solution is not unique, the thresholds below depend on this choice. Define the charge threshold θtc=ηc​μt−ωb\theta^{c}_{t}=\eta_{c}\mu_{t}-\omega_{b} and the discharge threshold θtd=μt/ηd+ωs\theta^{d}_{t}=\mu_{t}/\eta_{d}+\omega_{s}. By the optimality conditions, at uu the battery charges at full power in blocks where ut<θtcu_{t}<\theta^{c}_{t}, discharges at full power where ut>θtdu_{t}>\theta^{d}_{t}, is idle where θtc<ut<θtd\theta^{c}_{t}<u_{t}<\theta^{d}_{t}, and runs at partial power only where utu_{t} equals a threshold. The value μt\mu_{t} changes only when the storage is full or empty.

Theorem 4 (Safe clipping for batteries).

Suppose every price in uu and vv exceeds θ\theta, and that, for some optimal dual solution μ\mu of the LP at uu, every clipped block t∈𝒞t\in\mathcal{C} satisfies:

  1. (a)

    zuz_{u} does not charge or discharge at partial power in block tt;

  2. (b)

    if block tt is cut to the cap: when zuz_{u} discharges at full power there, p¯≥θtd\bar{p}\geq\theta^{d}_{t}; when zuz_{u} is idle there, p¯≥θtc\bar{p}\geq\theta^{c}_{t};

  3. (c)

    if block tt is raised to the floor: when zuz_{u} charges at full power there, p¯≤θtc\underline{p}\leq\theta^{c}_{t}; when zuz_{u} is idle there, p¯≤θtd\underline{p}\leq\theta^{d}_{t}.

Then zuz_{u} is a best schedule at vv. If it is the only best schedule at vv (or the selection rule picks it), then ℛclip​(p,u)=ℛraw​(p,u)\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,u)=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,u). Otherwise the solver may return a different schedule that is equally good at vv but not at the actual prices.

Because any optimal primal solution and any optimal dual solution of an LP satisfy complementary slackness together, the certificate may use any optimal dual solution, and it holds if it holds for at least one. Our computations use the dual solution returned by the solver, which makes the computed certificate conservative (Section 5). In words: after a forecast peak is cut to the cap, the raw schedule remains optimal as long as the cap is still above the price at which discharging in that block is worthwhile.

Corollary 2 (An unclipped partial-power block protects the peak).

Suppose zuz_{u} discharges at partial power in an unclipped block mm, and the storage stays strictly between empty and full from block mm to a clipped block tt in which zuz_{u} discharges at full power. Then condition (b) holds in block tt: θtd=θmd=um≤p¯\theta^{d}_{t}=\theta^{d}_{m}=u_{m}\leq\bar{p}.

So, after the full-power discharge blocks are clipped, the raw schedule remains optimal as long as the block where the battery runs at partial power, which sets the discharge threshold, is not clipped. A 1 MW/4 MWh battery discharges in about 16 to 23 of the 96 blocks on a typical day in our data. Once more blocks than this are clipped, the clipped set must include blocks that matter at the margin. Section 5 checks Theorem 4 on the trained forecasts and links it to how often clipping is costly.

Theorem 4 guarantees that the raw schedule stays optimal after projection, not that a solver returns it. A deterministic selection rule closes this gap.

Corollary 3 (Schedule-preserving selection).

Consider the rule that, after projection, deploys zuz_{u} whenever zuz_{u} is a best schedule at vv, and otherwise deploys a best schedule at vv. Under this rule, the deployed regret equals ℛraw​(p,u)\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,u) whenever zuz_{u} is a best schedule at vv, in particular whenever the conditions of Theorem 4 hold. Otherwise, its difference from ℛraw​(p,u)\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,u) satisfies the bounds of Proposition 3(iii).

The rule needs only the raw schedule and one check of its value at the projected forecast; the certificate of Theorem 4 gives a sufficient condition that can be read off the raw solution alone. Under this rule, projection can change the deployed regret only on days when the raw schedule is no longer optimal after projection. On those days, a natural refinement chooses, among the schedules that are optimal at vv, one that maximizes profit at the raw forecast uu (a lexicographic rule). It uses only information available before dispatch. It gives the same schedule as the rule of Corollary 3 whenever zuz_{u} is optimal at vv, provided that ties among schedules that are optimal at both vv and uu are broken in favor of zuz_{u}. Otherwise the two rules can pick different schedules that are equally good at both forecasts. Our implementation breaks such ties in favor of zuz_{u}: when zuz_{u} is optimal at vv, it is deployed directly. Section 5.5 evaluates both.

3.6 Training on projected forecasts and anchoring

An obvious idea is to train on the projected forecast, so that training matches how the forecast is used. Then the training loss is still an upper bound on regret, because ℓ⁡(Πℬ​(u),p)≥ℛclip​(p,u)\ell(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(u),p)\geq\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{clip}}(p,u) for every model output uu. But this does not by itself stop the drift.

Proposition 4 (Zero gradients after projection).

Let p^=Πℬ​(u)\hat{p}=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(u) and let 𝒞⁡(u)={t:ut>p¯​ or ​ut<p¯}\mathcal{C}(u)=\{t:u_{t}>\bar{p}\text{ or }u_{t}<\underline{p}\} be the blocks that are cut. Then ℓ​(Πℬ​(u),p)\ell(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(u),p) does not change with small changes in (ut)t∈𝒞⁡(u)(u_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{C}(u)}, so the gradient is zero in those blocks. If ut≥p¯u_{t}\geq\bar{p} for all tt, the loss is the same for all k≥0k\geq 0 along u+k​𝟏u+k\mathbf{1}, and equals the loss of the flat forecast p¯​𝟏\bar{p}\mathbf{1}.

Proposition 4 is about the direct gradient of the clipped blocks. A regression or a neural network shares parameters across blocks. Gradients from unclipped blocks can therefore still change the parameters and move clipped forecasts back inside the limits. But the loss gives no local signal from the clipped blocks themselves. In our experiments, this indirect effect was not enough to prevent the drift (Section 5).

Corollary 4 (Anchored training on projected forecasts).

Let a model give raw outputs uu. Form the anchored forecast

u~=u−H−1​(𝟏⊤​u)​ 1+L^​𝟏,\tilde{u}=u-H^{-1}(\mathbf{1}^{\top}u)\,\mathbf{1}+\hat{L}\mathbf{1}, (20)

whose daily level L^\hat{L} comes from a separate model, and deploy its projection p^=Πℬ​(u~)\hat{p}=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}(\tilde{u}). Train on ℓ⁡(p^,p)\ell(\hat{p},p) or Lσ​(p^,p)L_{\sigma}(\hat{p},p), evaluated at the deployed forecast p^\hat{p}. Then:

  1. (i)

    the training loss does not change when uu is shifted up or down, so training cannot learn a common level shift; this removes the freely learned level shift, but not every possible clipping error;

  2. (ii)

    for SPO+, the training loss ℓ⁡(p^,p)\ell(\hat{p},p), evaluated at the projected forecast p^\hat{p} that is used for the decision, is an upper bound on the regret after projection on every training day;

  3. (iii)

    the anchored forecast u~\tilde{u} has daily mean exactly L^\hat{L}, so its level error comes only from the separate level model, not from DFL training; by Proposition 1, it matters only through the factor 1−η1-\eta unless projection cuts it. After projection, clipping can change the daily mean of p^\hat{p}.

4 Data and test design

We now turn from theory to data. This section describes the market data and the battery, the forecasting methods we compare, and the test design and statistics used in Section 5.

4.1 Market, data and battery

We use 15-minute prices from the IEX day-ahead market (Indian Energy Exchange Limited, 2026), from 1 April 2022 to 31 August 2026 for the main study (1,614 calendar days); Section 5.4 uses later data. The regulator’s order of 1 April 2022 set a ceiling of Rs 12/kWh (Rs 12,000/MWh) for the day-ahead and real-time markets (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2022a), extended to further market segments on 6 May 2022 (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2022b). The April order does not state the first delivery day it affects. In our data, prices on 1 and 2 April 2022 still exceed Rs 12,000/MWh (up to Rs 20,000/MWh), but no later price does, so our panel starts on 3 April 2022. The ceiling was lowered to Rs 10/kWh for delivery from 4 April 2023 (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2023a), and the floor is zero. We use the ordinary day-ahead market, not its high-price segment, which has a separate ceiling of Rs 20/kWh. After a 90-day warm-up, the remaining 1,612 days give 1,522 delivery days, from 2 July 2022 to 31 August 2026. A day DD is evaluated only if days D−7D-7, D−6D-6, D−1D-1, DD and D+1D+1 all have complete data. This rule comes from the original design, in which every day also had to support a 48-hour schedule that uses day D+1D+1, and we keep it unchanged; all 1,522 days satisfy it.

The battery is 1 MW/4 MWh with η=0.85\eta=0.85 (ηc=ηd=0.85\eta_{c}=\eta_{d}=\sqrt{0.85}), a wear cost of Rs 1,062.5 per MWh cycled, split between buying and selling, an exchange fee of Rs 20/MWh for each (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2023b), and x¯=0\bar{x}=0. With perfect foresight (the “oracle”), it would earn Rs 65.82 lakh per MW-year. Section EC.3 reports a second test on the German day-ahead market.

4.2 Forecasting methods

All methods use only prices up to day D−1D-1. Every forecast is projected to the price limits and then used in the same 24-hour dispatch optimization.

  • •

    Seasonal naive: the prices of day D−1D-1.

  • •

    Regression: pD,t=β0+β1​pD−1,t+β2​pD−7,t+blockt+α1​sin⁡(2​π​m/12)+α2​cos⁡(2​π​m/12)+εp_{D,t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}p_{D-1,t}+\beta_{2}p_{D-7,t}+\text{block}_{t}+\alpha_{1}\sin(2\pi m/12)+\alpha_{2}\cos(2\pi m/12)+\varepsilon, estimated by least squares on all past data.

  • •

    Gradient boosting: histogram gradient boosting with settings fixed in advance. Inputs are lagged prices, block, day of week and month. Refit every week.

  • •

    LEAR-type LASSO (Lago et al., 2021; Tibshirani, 1996): one LASSO model for each block, on asinh-transformed prices. Inputs are all prices of day D−1D-1; the same block on days D−2D-2, D−3D-3 and D−7D-7; daily summary values; and day-of-week dummies. It uses the last 728 days, chooses variables by AIC, and is refit every week.

  • •

    EW3: the simple average of the projected regression, gradient boosting and LASSO forecasts (Bates and Granger, 1969).

  • •

    DFL methods. All are trained on the decision loss plus λ\lambda times the squared error of the forecast, using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). They start from the regression (the neural network is first trained on squared error) and are refit every 28 days on all past data, using batches of 16 days.

    • –

      V1: SPO+ with the regression’s inputs, trained on the forecast before projection.

    • –

      V2: as V1, but trained on the forecast after projection.

    • –

      V3: as V2, plus anchoring to the regression’s daily level (Algorithm 1).

    • –

      V4: a neural network (MLP, one hidden layer of 32 units) trained with SPO+, with anchoring and projection.

    • –

      V5: a perturbed Fenchel–Young method with anchoring, using 4 random draws.

4.3 Test design and statistics

Test design. We fixed the following before the tuning and holdout runs of the DFL models (see the last paragraph of this section).

  • •

    Periods. The validation year is 2 July 2022 to 30 June 2023 (364 days). It is used only for tuning. The holdout is 1 July 2023 to 31 August 2026 (1,158 days). It is used only for testing.

  • •

    Tuning. Each DFL method is tuned on its own grid, using only validation-year regret: λ∈{0.1,1}\lambda\in\{0.1,1\} and learning rate in {3×10−4,10−3,3×10−3}\{3\times 10^{-4},10^{-3},3\times 10^{-3}\}. For V5, we use λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, σ∈{300,1000}\sigma\in\{300,1000\} Rs/MWh and the same learning rates.

  • •

    Seeds. The chosen setting is run with three random seeds. The statistical methods have no settings to tune.

  • •

    Hindsight check. As an extra check, we also report the holdout regret of every setting for the two best DFL methods, as if the settings had been chosen with hindsight. This favors DFL, so it is a strict test of our conclusion.

On 39% of days there is more than one best schedule, mostly because many blocks clear at exactly the cap. The SPO+ loss depends on which one is used, so we fix the choice for each day.

Statistics. We compare methods by their daily regret differences. Confidence intervals come from a circular block bootstrap with 7-day blocks and 4,000 repetitions (Künsch, 1989; Politis and Romano, 1992). All holdout days are under the Rs 10 cap. Regret is given in lakh rupees per MW-year.

The LASSO and EW3 benchmarks were first found in earlier exploratory work on the full Indian sample. Earlier versions of this study, and our own exploratory runs of a linear SPO+ variant on 23 October 2026, also used the full evaluation range, including the later holdout. The holdout is therefore not a fully independent test of these choices. The DFL benchmark protocol was fixed in code later on 23 October 2026: the variants, tuning grids and selection rule before the tuning runs, and the seeds of the final runs before any holdout run. The German test was specified on 24 October 2026, before any German result; it checks the ranking in another market, but it cannot test the cost of projection, because German prices never reach their limits. The fresh-test protocol (Section 5.4) was written on 25 October 2026. Its days had already occurred, and we had checked the new data for completeness and computed the share of blocks at the cap, but no forecast or regret for those days had been computed; the protocol was fixed before the analysis, not registered in advance. The operating rules of Section 5.5 were fixed on 2 November 2026, each before its own comparison, but after the forecasting results were known, so their results are exploratory. For the fresh test and the operating rules, the original time-stamped protocol files are in the replication material. For the DFL benchmark and the German test, the design is recorded in the scripts that implement it, whose modification times precede the results. These times document the order of the work but are not independently certified.

5 Empirical results

This section first examines the predictions of Section 3 in the Indian data (Section 5.1). It then compares all forecasting methods on the holdout (Sections 5.2 and 5.3), reports a fresh test on later data (Section 5.4), evaluates operating rules based on the certificate of Theorem 4 (Section 5.5), and ends with the size of the gains (Section 5.6).

5.1 Level shift and projection in the data

At the regression forecast, the SPO+ helper problem charges 5.25 MWh per day, while the oracle charges 5.04. So Assumption 2 holds, and Theorem 3 predicts an upward loss-minimizing shift.

For the regression forecast, Table 1 gives the minimizer of the expected SPO+ loss Φ⁡(k)\Phi(k) for four efficiencies, each with its own oracle and wear-cost split, and Figure 1 plots Φ\Phi and the helper problem’s charged energy against the shift. We compute the minimizers by bisection on the condition in Theorem 3(ii), with the one-sided charged energies T∓T^{\mp} obtained by raising or lowering the buying cost by 0.01 Rs/MWh, to a tolerance of 1 Rs/MWh. The lower and upper ends of K⋆K^{\star} agree to within this tolerance, so the minimizer is effectively a single point. It is positive and rises from 324 to 2,496 Rs/MWh as η\eta goes from 0.80 to 0.95, while the matching cost increase δ⋆=2​(1−η)​k⋆\delta^{\star}=2(1-\eta)k^{\star} moves only from 130 to 250. The pure loss is almost flat in this direction: moving from k=0k=0 to k⋆k^{\star} lowers it by only 9 to 39 Rs per day, out of about 5,500. With the squared-error term of Corollary 1, as in V1 (in our units the tuned methods use λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 or λ=1\lambda=1), the loss-minimizing shift is much smaller: 152 to 235 Rs/MWh (λ=0.1\lambda=0.1) or 16 to 34 Rs/MWh (λ=1\lambda=1) above the squared-error level, and it does not grow as η→1\eta\to 1. This result does not apply to V2–V5 (Remark 3). Because the mean error of p^+k​𝟏\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1} is e¯+k\bar{e}+k, these shifts are on the same scale as the level errors in Tables 2 and 3, although they refer to a different forecast and sample.

  • •

    At every efficiency, the lower and upper ends of K⋆K^{\star} agree to within this accuracy, so the minimizer is a single point for practical purposes. It is positive and rises from 324 to 2,496 Rs/MWh as η\eta goes from 0.80 to 0.95.

  • •

    The matching cost increase δ⋆=2​(1−η)​k⋆\delta^{\star}=2(1-\eta)k^{\star} moves only from 130 to 250, while 1/(1−η)1/(1-\eta) grows four times.

  • •

    Moving from k=0k=0 to k⋆k^{\star} lowers the loss by only 9 to 39 Rs per day, out of about 5,500. The pure loss is almost flat in the level direction.

  • •

    For the objective of Corollary 1 (SPO+ plus squared error, both before projection, as in V1), the loss-minimizing shift is much smaller. In our units (thousand rupees, and thousand Rs/MWh for prices), the tuned methods use λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 or λ=1\lambda=1 (V1 uses λ=1\lambda=1). Then the loss-minimizing shift is 152 to 235 Rs/MWh (λ=0.1\lambda=0.1) or 16 to 34 Rs/MWh (λ=1\lambda=1) above the squared-error level. It does not grow as η→1\eta\to 1. This result does not apply to V2–V5 (Remark 3).

  • •

    A common scale. The mean error of the shifted forecast p^+k​𝟏\hat{p}+k\mathbf{1} relative to actual prices is e¯+k\bar{e}+k. So the shift of kλk_{\lambda} above −e¯-\bar{e} is exactly the mean forecast error relative to actual prices at the optimum. This is the same scale as the level errors in Tables 2 and 3. The numbers still refer to different forecasts (the regression here, V1 there) and different samples.

Table 2 retrains the tuned V1 (λ=1\lambda=1, 150 steps per refit) for three efficiencies. Its learned level moves up by about 2,400 to 2,500 Rs/MWh relative to actual prices in the validation year, far more than the loss-minimizing 16 to 34 Rs/MWh (Table 1).

Table 3 retrains V1 (seed 0) over the validation year with 150 to 5,000 steps per refit. At each refit it also applies an exact level correction: using only that refit’s training days, the level shift that minimizes the model’s own training objective (by bisection on the condition in Corollary 1), applied until the next refit. From 150 to 5,000 steps, the out-of-sample level error falls from 2,449 to 427 Rs/MWh and the regret from 6.60 to 4.58 lakh per MW-year, at a cost of about 35 thousand to one million training solves (half a minute to under seven minutes on one CPU core). Most of the drift in our main runs therefore comes from incomplete training. The level correction helps much less, because most of the level error appears only out of sample. In-sample level errors are at most about 520 Rs/MWh with 150 steps, but with few steps the fitted intercept and slopes give biased forecasts on new days: in one run (seed 1), the least-squares intercept fell from 5.9 to 1.2 thousand Rs/MWh between July and October 2022, while V1’s moved only from 6.0 to 4.8. Even with 5,000 steps and the correction, V1’s first-year regret (4.57) exceeds that of the regression (4.45) and of EW3 (4.08), although it is below that of anchored SPO+ with 150 steps (4.86).

To check that the ranking is not an artifact of under-training, we reran all five DFL variants (seed 0) with 2,000 steps per refit, 13 times the main budget, under a protocol fixed before the runs (Table 4). More training removes most of the first-year drift of the unanchored variants: the validation level error falls from +2,449 to +606 Rs/MWh for V1, reproducing Table 3, and from +2,637 to +821 for V2, and first-year regret falls from 6.60 to 4.62 and from 6.95 to 4.93. Holdout regret, however, barely moves for V1 to V3 (by at most 0.01) and rises for V4 (2.89 to 3.10) and V5 (3.49 to 3.66), apparently because longer training overfits the decision loss. For V4, the most seed-sensitive variant, the rise also holds for seeds 1 and 2 (2.88 to 3.11 and 2.91 to 3.01), and the three-seed mean, 3.07, remains worse than EW3 by 0.65 [0.50, 0.80]. Every variant remains worse than EW3 on the holdout, by at least 0.67 lakh per MW-year with every interval excluding zero, so under-training explains the early drift but not the ranking.

Table 5 uses the same V1 forecasts (150 steps, seeds 1 and 2) in different ways in the validation year. Relative to the regression (4.45), V1’s extra regret is 2.07. Removing projection lowers V1’s regret from 6.52 to 5.64, a change of 0.89 [0.24, 1.75]; giving the V1 forecasts the regression’s daily level lowers it to 4.93, with or without projection. The level and projection together therefore account for 1.59 of the 2.07 (77%), and the forecast shape for the remaining 0.48. How the 1.59 is split depends on the order of the changes: removing projection first attributes 0.89 to projection and 0.71 to the level, while correcting the level first leaves nothing for projection. This is a counterfactual decomposition, not a unique causal split; what is clear is that projection is costly here only because the level is too high.

Table 6 groups the same days by the share of V1’s forecast blocks that are above the cap. Projection costs nothing on days with up to 10% of blocks clipped, and almost nothing up to 25%. Above 25% the cost rises steeply. Theorem 4 and Corollary 2 explain this pattern. The battery discharges in about 16 to 23 blocks a day. As long as the block where it runs at partial power is not clipped, clipping its full-power discharge blocks leaves the raw schedule optimal. When more blocks are clipped than the battery discharges in, clipping reaches the blocks that matter at the margin.

When the cap fell from Rs 12,000 to Rs 10,000/MWh on 4 April 2023, prices reached it more often, but the cost of projection did not rise: it fell for V1, whose early level drift faded, and stayed near zero for the other forecasts (Section EC.4). This descriptive evidence is consistent with the theory: projection is costly when the forecast level is too high.

For each day and V1 forecast (seeds 1 and 2), we solved the LP at the raw forecast, took the energy values μt\mu_{t} from the solver, and checked the conditions of Theorem 4 (Table 7). The thresholds explain every raw schedule exactly, and no violation was observed: on all 2,312 day-seeds where the conditions hold, the raw schedule is still optimal after projection, and the two-sided bound of Proposition 3(iii) holds on all 3,044 day-seeds. The conditions are conservative. On days with up to 25% of blocks clipped they fail on about 40% of days, mostly (518 days) because of the condition for idle blocks, yet the raw schedule stopped being optimal on only 2 of 1,500 such days. When more than 25% of blocks are clipped, clipping almost always reaches a partial-power block (94%), and the raw schedule stops being optimal on 40% of days; this is where the cost of projection in Table 6 comes from.

Training on projected forecasts did not stop the shift: V2 shifts at least as much as V1 (mean level error +755 against +643 Rs/MWh, and 9.2% against 4.3% of forecast blocks above the cap; Figure 2), consistent with Proposition 4 and Remark 3. The anchored methods take their level from the regression, and their results depend little on the learning rate (validation regret 4.90 to 4.98 across all settings, against 6.60 to 32.48 for V1).

In the German test (Section EC.3), Assumption 2 also holds (4.08 against 2.58 MWh per day), and unconstrained SPO+ moved its level up by only about 3 EUR/MWh. No price was cut, and V1 performed the same as its anchored version.

5.2 Main comparison

Table 8 gives the regret of all methods in the validation year and on the holdout. On the holdout, every DFL method is worse than EW3, with every interval excluding zero, by at least +0.47+0.47 lakh per MW-year. The best DFL method, the anchored neural-network SPO+ (V4), outperforms the regression it starts from by 0.28 [0.07, 0.48]. It is about as good as gradient boosting and worse than the LASSO. On the holdout, the linear SPO+ methods are about as good as the regression, and the Fenchel–Young method is the worst. Different random seeds change the results by at most 0.03. Figure 3 shows the holdout comparison.

Choosing the DFL settings with hindsight, on the holdout itself, does not change the result. The best anchored linear SPO+ then reaches 3.09 and the best neural-network SPO+ 2.89, against 2.43 for EW3.

Adding DFL forecasts to the average does not help much:

  • •

    EW3 plus the neural-network SPO+ gives 2.39, a change of −0.04-0.04 [−0.09-0.09, +0.01+0.01];

  • •

    using the neural-network SPO+ instead of the regression gives 2.38, a change of −0.04-0.04 [−0.11-0.11, +0.02+0.02].

Weights chosen from past profit or past squared error also do not outperform equal weights. This matches the known finding that equal weights are hard to beat (Smith and Wallis, 2009).

5.3 Different battery designs

Table 9 changes the battery’s duration, efficiency, wear cost and start-and-end level. For each design we recompute the oracle and all schedules, and we retrain the best DFL method (V4). The ranking does not change. EW3 has lower holdout regret than V4 in every design, and the interval excludes zero in 8 of 8 designs. The gap is between 0.21 lakh per MW-year (double wear cost) and 0.60 (battery half full at the start and end of the day). EW3 is also better than each of the three forecasts it averages, in every design.

5.4 A fresh test on new Indian data

After the analysis above was complete, we obtained IEX day-ahead prices for 1 September to 24 October 2026. Before computing any forecast or regret for these days, we fixed a test design (Section 4.3): the same battery, methods and settings, three seeds and no re-tuning; the same evaluation rule and statistics; a primary comparison of EW3 with the best DFL method (V4); and a reading rule, under which the ranking is “confirmed” if EW3 has lower mean regret than every DFL method, and “significantly confirmed” against a method only if the 95% interval excludes zero. Because the evaluation rule needs day D+1D+1, the test covers the 53 delivery days from 1 September to 23 October 2026. Prices for 1–27 September were already in our original, unused data files; the rest are new. Rerunning the whole pipeline on the extended data reproduces all earlier forecasts exactly, except the neural network, whose earlier holdout regret changes by at most 0.005.

This period is very different from the main holdout: 62% of blocks clear at the cap, against 17%, and the oracle profit is Rs 86.9 lakh per MW-year. Table 10 gives the results. EW3 has lower regret than V4, but the difference, +0.42+0.42 [−0.45-0.45, +1.35+1.35], is not significant, and although EW3 has lower mean regret than every DFL method, it is significantly better only than V5. The regression alone has the lowest regret (2.67, against 2.90 for EW3), although the difference is not significant, and four of the five DFL methods are significantly worse than the regression they start from (for V2 the interval just touches zero). So in this fresh, heavily capped period no DFL method outperforms the regression or the equal-weight average, but the data do not single out EW3 as the best statistical method, and the intervals are wide.

On the fresh days, with long training windows, V1’s level no longer drifts upward (mean level error -93 Rs/MWh), and its cost of projection is small: +0.15+0.15 [0.000.00, +0.33+0.33]. V2, which is trained after projection, is the only method with an upward level (+230 Rs/MWh), with 55% of its forecast blocks above the cap, consistent with Proposition 4. No violation of Theorem 4 or of the bound of Proposition 3(iii) was observed. For V1, the raw schedule stays optimal after projection on every fresh day; the small cost of projection comes from ties, when the solver picks an equally good schedule that does worse at actual prices. This is the case covered by the selection clause of Theorem 4.

5.5 Using the certificate in operation

What should an operator do with a forecast that will be clipped? The comparisons summarized here are exploratory: the rules were designed after the forecasting results were known and are evaluated on periods already used in the study, although each rule was fixed before its own comparison. Section EC.5 gives the rules and the full results (Tables EC.2 and EC.3).

A rule that anchors a forecast only when the certificate of Theorem 4 fails lowers the first-year regret of the unanchored variants V1 and V2 from 6.55 to 5.62 and from 6.95 to 5.72. Anchoring on every day lowers it further, to 4.95 and 5.28, because a high level costs money even when the raw schedule remains optimal after clipping. On the holdout the rule changes regret by at most 0.02. For the statistical forecasts the certificate holds on 92% to 100% of days and the rule changes almost nothing, but in the fresh test anchoring the LASSO to the regression’s level raised its regret by 0.67 [0.04, 1.53].

The raw schedule stays optimal after clipping on 97.8% to 100% of days for every method. Keeping it whenever it remains optimal (Corollary 3) makes the deployed regret equal to the raw regret on those days. The effect on average regret is small and goes both ways (between −0.04-0.04 and +0.03+0.03 on the holdout), and in the fresh test it lowers V1’s regret by 0.15 [0.00, 0.33]. On the remaining days, choosing the optimal schedule that the raw forecast prefers lowers first-year regret by 0.40 [0.13, 0.75] for V1 and 0.55 [0.22, 0.95] for V2. Even with these rules, the best DFL variant stays behind EW3 on the holdout, by 0.46 [0.34, 0.58].

In practice, then, the level of a decision-focused forecast should be anchored, the level of a well-calibrated statistical forecast should be left alone, the certificate shows on which days clipping may change the schedule, and ties should be broken in favor of the raw schedule.

5.6 Size of the gains

For a 1 MW/4 MWh battery in India, EW3 earns Rs 0.74 lakh per year more than the regression on the holdout, and Rs 0.47 lakh more than the best tuned DFL method. These are 23% of the regression’s holdout regret and 16% of the best DFL method’s. In the first year, unanchored DFL would have lost Rs 1.69 lakh more than anchored DFL (validation-year regret of 6.55 against 4.86 lakh per MW-year). These gains are meaningful relative to the regret a method can reduce (Proposition 2), but small relative to the value of the battery: the advantage of EW3 over the best DFL method is about 0.7% of the perfect-foresight profit on the holdout (Rs 66.7 lakh per MW-year). The value of perfect information is the same for every method. For a 100 MW plant, the gain of EW3 over the regression would be about Rs 0.74 crore per year. This is only a rough figure, because a plant that large would affect prices.

6 Implications and limitations

This section brings the theoretical and empirical results together, discusses what they mean for practice, and states the limitations of the study.

6.1 Summary of the evidence

The results separate four effects. Under Assumption 2, the losses favor a forecast level that is too high, but with the squared-error term used in training this effect is small (Theorem 3, Corollary 1, Table 1). The much larger level error early in the sample comes mostly from limited training: more steps per refit reduce it from about 2,450 to about 430 Rs/MWh (Table 3), and a larger budget for all variants leaves the ranking unchanged (Table 4). A high level hurts mainly after projection flattens the forecast peaks. When the conditions of Theorem 4 hold, the raw schedule stays optimal, and in our data projection was costly mostly when more than about a quarter of the blocks were clipped (Tables 5, 6 and 7). Out of sample, no DFL variant did better than the equal-weight statistical average on the holdout or in any of the eight battery designs, and none did better than the regression or the average in the fresh test (Tables 8, 9 and 10). More training deals with the second effect and anchoring with the third, but neither was enough for the tested DFL variants to beat the statistical benchmarks. Table 11 lists the robustness checks and separates the results that follow from the theory from those that depend on the implementations we tested.

6.2 Implications for practice

Before using a decision-focused forecast, it is worth checking which directions the training loss barely sees. For a battery this is the price level; for other problems with a conservation constraint it is the conserved total (Theorem 1). Any later step that is not neutral in that direction, such as clipping to price limits, can turn an error in it into lost profit.

Without anchoring, a decision-focused forecast can end up with a level that is far too high, especially early on. A high level acts like an extra buying cost and, after clipping, flattens the forecast peaks; in our data these two effects explain most of the extra regret of unanchored SPO+ (Table 5). Taking the level from a separate model removes the problem at little cost, and in the first year it worked better to do this every day than only when the certificate failed. Changing the level of a well-calibrated statistical forecast, on the other hand, can make it worse. When forecasts are clipped, it also helps to keep the raw schedule whenever it remains optimal (Section 5.5).

Decision-focused methods should also be compared with several good statistical forecasts and their simple average, using a design fixed in advance. On the holdout, the anchored neural-network SPO+ did 9% better than its own regression but 0.47 lakh per MW-year worse than the average, and in the fresh test the regression did best.

Two further remarks.
