When all forecasts lead to the same schedule, that schedule is also optimal for their average, so averaging can change the decision only on days when the forecasts disagree; in our data, this is where its gain comes from (Section EC.4). And price caps on their own do not make decision-focused learning fail. The harm comes from clipping forecasts to the cap, which is the operator’s choice.

6.3 Limitations

Some of the evidence is less independent than we would like. EW3 and the LASSO came out of earlier exploratory work on the same data, and exploratory SPO+ runs came before the benchmark protocol was fixed (Section 4.3). The holdout is therefore a fair test of the DFL variants but not of the choice of EW3. The fresh test does not depend on these choices, but it covers only 53 days and does not show that EW3 beats the regression. Its protocol was written after those days had passed, and its first 27 days were already in our original, unused data files. The operating-rule comparisons are exploratory, and German prices never reach their limits.

On the theory side, the convexity and throughput-matching results hold in general, but the upward shift needs Assumption 2, which holds in our data but need not hold elsewhere. Corollary 1 covers training before projection (V1) only, and we give no theory of how training evolves. Theorem 4 is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one; Proposition 3(iii) bounds the change in regret, but we have no lower bound that depends only on the share of clipped blocks.

Finally, published DFL implementations (Smets et al., 2025a; Smets et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2025; Alkhulaifi et al., 2026) and larger networks may perform differently, and we do not replicate them, although Theorem 3 applies to any model trained on these losses without anchoring. We study a small battery that takes prices as given, in one day-ahead market with a binding cap, and Theorem 1 is tested only for batteries.

7 Conclusion

Decision-focused learning trains forecasts for the decisions they lead to, but forecasts are often transformed before they reach the decision. We showed three things for problems with a conservation-type constraint. Decision-focused losses identify the forecast level only weakly. When the helper problem inside the loss has excess throughput, as it does in our data, the loss prefers a higher level. A squared-error term keeps this preference small, but limited training can leave the level much higher. Projecting such a forecast onto a price cap can then erase profitable spreads and increase regret, even as prediction error falls. We bounded the change in regret caused by post-processing, gave a dual-threshold certificate under which a raw-optimal schedule remains optimal after clipping, and showed that anchoring removes the freely learned level shift. On the Indian day-ahead market, an equal-weight average of three statistical forecasts outperformed every DFL variant we tested on the holdout. On 53 later days with most prices at the cap, no variant outperformed the regression or the average, although most differences from the average were not significant; a German test gave the same point ranking. In capped markets, decision-focused forecasts should be anchored before use and benchmarked against strong statistical forecasts. Natural next steps are to extend the theory to batteries that trade in several markets and to other conservation-constrained problems, and to test the results over a longer period of new data and in other markets where caps bind.

Proof of Proposition 3. Since J⁡(v,z)−J⁡(u,z)=Δ​(v−u)⊤​q​(z)J(v,z)-J(u,z)=\Delta(v-u)^{\top}q(z) and v−uv-u is zero outside 𝒞\mathcal{C},

(ii) The last sum is at least −Δ∑t∈𝒞|ut−vt||qt(zu)−qt(z)|-\Delta\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}}|u_{t}-v_{t}|\,|q_{t}(z_{u})-q_{t}(z)|, so under the condition the right-hand side is positive for every other z∈𝒱z\in\mathcal{V}. and u−vu-v is zero outside 𝒞\mathcal{C}. □\square

Proof of Theorem 4. Because all prices exceed θ\theta, the LP is exact at uu and at vv (Lemma 1), and the optimality (KKT) conditions of the LP are necessary and sufficient. Let μ\mu be the optimal dual solution for which the conditions of the theorem hold, with μt\mu_{t} the multiplier of the storage equation of block tt. Since zuz_{u} and μ\mu are optimal primal and dual solutions, they satisfy complementary slackness together. At a price vector π\pi, the optimality conditions are of two kinds. For every block tt,

ct=c¯​if​πt<θtc,ct=0​if​πt>θtc,dt=d¯​if​πt>θtd,dt=0​if​πt<θtd,c_{t}=\bar{c}\ \text{if}\ \pi_{t}<\theta^{c}_{t},\quad c_{t}=0\ \text{if}\ \pi_{t}>\theta^{c}_{t},\quad d_{t}=\bar{d}\ \text{if}\ \pi_{t}>\theta^{d}_{t},\quad d_{t}=0\ \text{if}\ \pi_{t}<\theta^{d}_{t},

with fractional power only where πt\pi_{t} equals the corresponding threshold. For every storage level xtx_{t},

μt+1−μt≥0​if​xt=B,μt+1−μt≤0​if​xt=0,μt+1−μt=0​otherwise.\mu_{t+1}-\mu_{t}\geq 0\ \text{if}\ x_{t}=B,\qquad\mu_{t+1}-\mu_{t}\leq 0\ \text{if}\ x_{t}=0,\qquad\mu_{t+1}-\mu_{t}=0\ \text{otherwise}.

The storage conditions do not involve prices, and at vv prices change only in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In a block cut to the cap, the price falls from utu_{t} to p¯\bar{p}. Full charging remains consistent, because a lower price makes charging more attractive. Full discharging remains consistent if p¯≥θtd\bar{p}\geq\theta^{d}_{t}. Idling remains consistent if p¯≥θtc\bar{p}\geq\theta^{c}_{t}, since the price stays below θtd\theta^{d}_{t}. Fractional power is excluded by (a). The case of a block raised to the floor is symmetric. So (zu,μ)(z_{u},\mu) satisfies the optimality conditions at vv, and zuz_{u} is a best schedule at vv. □\square

Proof of Corollary 2. Fractional discharge at mm means um=θmdu_{m}=\theta^{d}_{m}. If the storage is strictly between its limits from mm to tt, the storage conditions give μ\mu constant on these blocks, so

θtd=μt/ηd+ωs=μm/ηd+ωs=θmd=um≤p¯,\theta^{d}_{t}=\mu_{t}/\eta_{d}+\omega_{s}=\mu_{m}/\eta_{d}+\omega_{s}=\theta^{d}_{m}=u_{m}\leq\bar{p},

where the last inequality holds because block mm is not clipped. □\square

Appendix EC.2 Implementation details

Dispatch optimization. Each dispatch problem is first solved as a linear program with HiGHS; if the solution charges and discharges in the same block, it is re-solved as a mixed-integer program (see below). During training, the linear-programming model is kept in memory and only the prices change between solves. For evaluation, each problem is solved from scratch, so that ties are broken in the same way for every method. Both ways give the same profit to within 4×10−114\times 10^{-11}.

No simultaneous charging and discharging. By Lemma 1, the LP is exact when every price exceeds θ=−(ωb+ηωs)/(1−η)\theta=-(\omega_{b}+\eta\omega_{s})/(1-\eta). We solve the LP and, if a solution charges and discharges in the same block, re-solve with binary variables yty_{t} (ct≤c¯​ytc_{t}\leq\bar{c}\,y_{t}, dt≤d¯​(1−yt)d_{t}\leq\bar{d}(1-y_{t})). For the Indian base battery (θ≈−6,780\theta\approx-6{,}780 Rs/MWh), all prices exceeded θ\theta in every audited solve, so the LP was exact and no re-solve was needed: the oracle and all forecast schedules on all evaluation days; the SPO+ helper problems for the regression and V1–V4; 6,088 Fenchel–Young draws; 211,200 training-time solves of V1, V2 and V5 in the validation year (lowest price −4,101-4{,}101 Rs/MWh); and the level searches of Table 1 (lowest price −3,824-3{,}824 Rs/MWh, at least 1,107 Rs/MWh above θ\theta at every efficiency). Realized prices and projected forecasts are never negative, and in the level-correction bisection of Table 3 the final brackets lie where all helper prices exceed θ\theta. With η=0.80\eta=0.80 (θ≈−4,930\theta\approx-4{,}930), none of 70,400 training-time solves was affected. With no wear cost, θ\theta is only about −250-250 Rs/MWh, and 0.34% of training-time helper solves charged and discharged at once; we reran this design with the exact re-solve in every solve, and 1,524 of 145,249 solves needed it (Table 9). In Germany (θ≈−77\theta\approx-77 EUR/MWh; 16 evaluation hours below it), the LP oracle charged and discharged at once on 3 of 2,184 days and the gradient boosting schedule on 2 days, so all German results use the exact re-solve everywhere, including all training-time helper problems; during training it was needed in 0.013% to 0.021% of solves.

Code checks. On 200 randomly chosen Indian days, ℓ⁡(p,p)=0\ell(p,p)=0 exactly, and ℓ⁡(p^,p)−ℛraw​(p,p^)≥35.65\ell(\hat{p},p)-\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{raw}}(p,\hat{p})\geq 35.65 rupees for the projected forecast p^\hat{p}, so the loss is always above the regret. With the oracle schedule fixed, the SPO+ subgradient passes the convexity check (directional derivative at least g⊤​vg^{\top}v) in all 400 random directions, to within 2×10−112\times 10^{-11}, and the derivative with respect to the level matches Theorem 3(i) to machine precision.

DFL training. Model outputs are in units of Rs 1,000/MWh (India) or EUR 10/MWh (Germany). The loss is SPO+ (or Fenchel–Young) plus λ\lambda times the mean squared error of the forecast that is used. Gradients are set to zero in blocks cut by the projection. For anchored methods, they are also centered within the day. Adam uses β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999). The first refit takes 400 steps from the starting model. Each later 28-day refit takes 150 steps. Each step uses 16 training days drawn at random from all past data. The neural network (MLP) has 20 (India) or 22 (Germany) inputs per block: lagged prices, summary values of day D−1D-1, block, day of week and month terms, and in Germany the load and wind-plus-solar forecasts. It has one hidden layer of 32 tanh units and is first trained for 3,000 steps on squared error. The Fenchel–Young gradient averages 4 random normal draws per day.

Chosen settings. India: V1 and V2 (λ,lr)=(1,3×10−3)(\lambda,\text{lr})=(1,3\times 10^{-3}); V3 (0.1,10−3)(0.1,10^{-3}); V4 (1,10−3)(1,10^{-3}); V5 (λ,σ,lr)=(0.1,1000,3×10−4)(\lambda,\sigma,\text{lr})=(0.1,1000,3\times 10^{-4}). Germany: V1 (λ,lr)=(0.1,3×10−3)(\lambda,\text{lr})=(0.1,3\times 10^{-3}); V3 (λ,lr)=(0.1,3×10−3)(\lambda,\text{lr})=(0.1,3\times 10^{-3}); V4 (λ,lr)=(1,3×10−3)(\lambda,\text{lr})=(1,3\times 10^{-3}).

Code and data. The IEX data are public market data, and the German data are the public benchmark dataset of Lago et al. (2021). All code (data preparation, dispatch optimization, forecasts, DFL training and evaluation) is included in the replication package that accompanies the submission.

Appendix EC.3 Second test: German day-ahead market

Purpose of the test. The main results use one market, and EW3 was first found in exploratory work on the same data. To check whether the ranking holds elsewhere, we repeat the comparison on a second market. We set up this test after seeing the Indian results but before seeing any German result. German prices never reach their limits, so this test checks the ranking and whether the level shift appears. It cannot check the loss caused by a binding cap.

Data and battery. We use the public benchmark dataset of Lago et al. (2021) for the EPEX day-ahead market (Germany–Austria). It has hourly prices from 9 January 2012 to 31 December 2017, and the load forecast and wind-plus-solar forecast published before the auction. The price limits are −500-500 and +3,000+3{,}000 EUR/MWh, and they never bind: actual prices range from −222-222 to 210 EUR/MWh. A day has H=24H=24 blocks with Δ=1\Delta=1. The battery is the same as in India. Its wear cost is EUR 12 per MWh cycled (the Indian value in euros) and the fee is EUR 0.25/MWh for buying and for selling. With perfect foresight, the battery would earn EUR 9,541 per MW-year.

Methods and design. The methods are those of Section 4, with three changes:

  • •

    every model also uses the load and wind-plus-solar forecasts for day DD;

  • •

    the regression also has a weekend dummy and day-of-year terms;

  • •

    the LASSO also uses these forecasts for days DD, D−1D-1 and D−7D-7.

Because the limits never bind, V2 is the same as V1. We therefore run V1, V3 and V4. We drop V5 because it was the weakest method in India. The validation year is 2015 and the holdout is 2016–2017 (731 days), the same test period as in Lago et al. (2021). Tuning, seeds and statistics are as in India.

Results. Table EC.1 and Figure EC.1 give the results. The ranking is the same as in India.

  • •

    EW3 has the lowest holdout regret, EUR 2,257 per MW-year. The LASSO is not significantly different from it.

  • •

    The best DFL method is again the anchored neural-network SPO+, at 2,425. This is +167+167 [−-9, 346] above EW3. The point estimate favors EW3, but the interval includes zero, so in Germany this gap is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The linear SPO+ methods are about 430 to 450 above EW3, and these gaps are significant.

  • •

    All three DFL methods outperform the regression they start from, by 339 to 617 EUR per MW-year. (In India, only the neural-network method does.) So, without a binding cap, DFL improves on its starting model, but it does not outperform an average of good statistical forecasts.

Level shift. At the regression forecast, the SPO+ helper problem charges 4.08 MWh per day, while the oracle charges 2.58. So Theorem 3 predicts an upward shift. Unconstrained SPO+ did move its level up compared with its starting regression, by 3.1 EUR/MWh in the validation year. But the shift was small compared with German prices, no hour ever went outside the price limits, and V1 and its anchored version perform the same on the holdout (2,689 and 2,702 EUR per MW-year). The upward shift is observed, but its effect on regret is not statistically significant here.

Appendix EC.4 Other results

Conditions under which averaging helps. For any z∈ℱz\in\mathcal{F}, the set N⁡(z)={π:z∈arg​maxz′∈ℱ⁡J​(π,z′)}N(z)=\{\pi:z\in\argmax_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}}J(\pi,z^{\prime})\} equals ⋂z′∈𝒱{π:Δ​π⊤​(q⁡(z)−q⁡(z′))≥C⁡(z)−C⁡(z′)}\bigcap_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\{\pi:\Delta\pi^{\top}(q(z)-q(z^{\prime}))\geq C(z)-C(z^{\prime})\}, the normal cone of zz used in Proposition 3(i). It is an intersection of half-spaces, so it is convex. So, if zz is a best schedule for each forecast, it is also a best schedule for any weighted average of them.

Gain from averaging and disagreement between forecasts (India, full sample). For each day, we measure how much the three forecasts in EW3 disagree by the average of Δ​∑t|q^k,t−q^l,t|\Delta\sum_{t}|\hat{q}_{k,t}-\hat{q}_{l,t}| over the three pairs. This uses forecasts only. The gain of EW3 over the mean regret of its three component forecasts, in Rs lakh per MW-year with 95% bootstrap intervals, grows with disagreement:

  • •

    low disagreement (bottom third of days): 0.23 [0.17, 0.29];

  • •

    middle third: 0.52 [0.41, 0.63];

  • •

    high disagreement (top third): 1.18 [0.99, 1.41].

The gain does not change in a clear way with the oracle’s local dual margin (0.57, 0.71, 0.66). EW3 has lower regret than the mean regret of its three component forecasts on 75% of days.

Other methods tested. Two other corrections did not help. Adjusting the trading costs online, which by Lemma 2 is the same as rescaling and shifting the forecast, lowers regret by at most 0.07 lakh, even with hindsight. Choosing the averaging weights online from past profit or past squared error does not outperform equal weights (full sample; differences +0.04+0.04 [−0.01-0.01, +0.09+0.09] and +0.01+0.01 [−0.03-0.03, +0.04+0.04]).

The 2023 cap change.

The cap fell from Rs 12,000 to Rs 10,000/MWh on 4 April 2023, which changes how often prices reach the cap. Over the 90 days before and after the change, the share of realized blocks at the cap rose from 13.1% to 18.1% (8.6% and 17.2% over all days under each cap). The cost of projection did not follow the cap. For V1 (seeds 1 and 2), the share of forecast blocks above the cap fell from 15.0% to 3.1% and the cost of projection from +3.02+3.02 to −0.05-0.05 lakh per MW-year, because its early level drift faded as training data accumulated. For the statistical forecasts and the anchored V3, clipping rose somewhat after the change (to at most 9.1% of blocks), but the cost of projection stayed within ±0.1\pm 0.1 lakh per MW-year in both windows. Because the change almost coincides with the end of the first year, these comparisons are descriptive; they do not identify an effect of the cap. They are, however, consistent with the theory: projection is costly when the forecast level is too high, not just because the cap binds more often.

Appendix EC.5 Operating rules: details

Section 5.5 summarizes these comparisons; this section gives the full results. Table EC.2 compares always clipping (P), never clipping (U), always anchoring before clipping (A) and the certificate-based switch (C), which clips when the conditions of Theorem 4 hold and otherwise anchors before clipping. Table EC.3 compares the solver’s own choice among tied schedules (P) with schedule-preserving selection (S, Corollary 3) and lexicographic selection (L), which on the days when the raw schedule is no longer optimal picks, among the schedules that are optimal at the clipped forecast, one that maximizes profit at the raw forecast. Rules C, S and L were each fixed before their comparison, and remaining ties under L are broken in favor of the raw schedule.
